name: Louis XIV
info: Louis XIV, known as the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 to 1715, a reign of 72 years that centralised royal authority at Versailles, made France the leading power in Europe and was marked by costly wars and the persecution of Protestants.

facts.born: 5 September 1638 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, as Louis Dieudonné; son of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, of the House of Bourbon
facts.died: 1 September 1715 at Versailles, of gangrene, four days before his 77th birthday; buried in the Basilica of Saint-Denis
facts.role: King of France from 14 May 1643 until his death in 1715; under the regency of his mother Anne of Austria and the chief minister Cardinal Mazarin until 1661, then ruling without a chief minister
facts.known: the longest reign of any monarch; the consolidation of absolute monarchy; the palace of Versailles and its court; the Franco-Dutch War, the Nine Years' War and the War of the Spanish Succession; the revocation of the Edict of Nantes; Colbert's financial and commercial reforms; patronage of Molière, Racine, Lully and Le Brun

t: Louis became king at four, lived through the Fronde as a child, and from 1661 ruled without a chief minister, drawing the nobility to his court at Versailles and weakening their independent power.

France was the leading European power under him, but his wars against shifting alliances strained its finances, and the long war over the Spanish succession ended in 1713 and 1714 with France in major debt.

He banned Protestant worship by the Edict of Fontainebleau in 1685, after years of persecution and the quartering of dragoons in Protestant homes; historians still dispute how much the departure of some 200,000 Huguenots harmed France.
dyk: Louis was an eager dancer who performed 80 roles in 40 major ballets, among them Neptune and Apollo in Molière's Les Amants magnifiques in 1670.
ev: Louis is born at Saint-Germain-en-Laye after 23 years of his parents' marriage and is named Louis Dieudonné
He becomes king at the age of four on the death of Louis XIII, with his mother Anne of Austria as sole regent and Cardinal Mazarin as chief minister
After Mazarin's death Louis declares that he will rule without a chief minister
France invades the Dutch Republic, beginning the Franco-Dutch War, which ends with the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678
The royal court moves officially to the Palace of Versailles
The Edict of Fontainebleau revokes the Edict of Nantes and ends the toleration of Protestants in France
The Peace of Utrecht ends the War of the Spanish Succession, leaving Philip V on the Spanish throne
Louis dies at Versailles and is succeeded by his five-year-old great-grandson, Louis XV

sections.early:
Louis was born on 5 September 1638 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the son of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria. His parents had been married for 23 years, and his mother had suffered four stillbirths between 1619 and 1631, so leading contemporaries regarded him as a divine gift and his birth as a miracle. He was named Louis Dieudonné, "Louis the God-given", and bore the title of the heir apparent, Dauphin. His relationship with his mother was uncommonly affectionate for the time, and it was she who gave him his belief in the absolute and divine power of his rule. In his childhood he was cared for by governesses, and in 1646 Nicolas V de Villeroy became his tutor.

Sensing his death near in the spring of 1643, Louis XIII decreed that a regency council would govern for his four-year-old son, with Anne at its head. He died on 14 May 1643. On 18 May Anne had the will annulled by the Parlement of Paris and became sole regent. She appointed Cardinal Mazarin chief minister and continued the policies of Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu. In 1648 she and Mazarin negotiated the Peace of Westphalia, which ended the Thirty Years' War and gave France the Habsburg lands and claims in Alsace and sovereignty over the Three Bishoprics of Metz, Verdun and Toul.
sections.rise:
The same year a civil war, the Fronde, broke out. When Anne and Mazarin tried in 1648 to tax the members of the Parlement of Paris, the members refused and Mazarin had some of them arrested, among them Pierre Broussel; Paris rioted and Anne had to free him. On the night of 9 to 10 February 1651, when Louis was twelve, a mob broke into the palace and was led into his bedchamber, where he feigned sleep. The royal family was driven out of Paris twice, and at one point Louis and Anne were held under virtual arrest in the palace. These years planted in Louis a hatred of Paris and a distrust of the higher aristocracy. The Fronde ended in 1653 when Mazarin returned from exile. Louis was declared of age on 7 September 1651. Anne and Mazarin sent away Mazarin's niece Marie Mancini, with whom Louis had fallen in love, and in 1660 he married Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV of Spain, under the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659.

When Mazarin died in March 1661, Louis astonished his court by declaring that he would govern himself: "It is now time that I govern them myself." He then moved against Nicolas Fouquet, the Superintendent of Finances, whose wealth and ambition worried him. Fouquet was charged with embezzlement and the Parlement sentenced him to exile; Louis altered the sentence to life imprisonment. In 1665 he named Jean-Baptiste Colbert Controller-General of Finances.
sections.deeds:
Colbert reorganised taxation and put the accounts in order: the deficit of 1661 turned into a surplus by 1666, and interest on the debt fell from 52 million to 24 million livres. His mercantilist administration founded new industries, among them the Lyon silk manufacturers and the Gobelins tapestry manufactory, and invited foreign craftsmen to France. Michel le Tellier and his son Louvois reorganised the army into a professional, disciplined force. The Great Ordinance of Civil Procedure of 1667, the Code Louis, imposed a uniform civil procedure across the kingdom and required baptismal, marriage and death records to be kept in state registers. The Great Ordinance on the Colonies of 1685, the Code Noir, sanctioned slavery while prohibiting the separation of families, and allowed only Roman Catholics to own slaves.

Louis made Versailles the seat of government, and the court moved there officially on 6 May 1682. Nobles who wanted pensions and privileges had to wait constantly on the king, and he used court ritual and censorship to watch them, so that the old military aristocracy became ceremonial courtiers while commoners and the newer nobility of the robe filled executive posts. He patronised Molière, Racine, La Fontaine, Lully, Le Brun and Le Nôtre, and the Canal du Midi, 240 km long, was built. His image as the Sun King was spread by portraits, medals, statues and tapestries, and Colbert set up a system to create it.
sections.opponents:
Warfare defined Louis's foreign policy, impelled by his ambition for glory and power. He claimed Spanish territory in the War of Devolution of 1667 and invaded the Dutch Republic in May 1672; the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 left his two chief aims, destroying the Republic and conquering the Spanish Netherlands, unachieved. His annexations after 1679, including Strasbourg in 1681, alienated much of Europe. In 1684 he had Algiers and Tripoli bombarded and sent a punitive mission against Genoa. In the Nine Years' War, which began in 1688, French forces pursued a scorched earth policy in southwestern Germany, the Devastation of the Palatinate, and in 1695 Louis ordered the bombardment of Brussels, which destroyed more than 4,000 buildings. Napoleon later called it "as barbarous as it was useless".

In 1681 Louis banned Protestant emigration and began quartering dragoons in Protestant homes, which subjected Protestants to ruin and atrocious abuse; between 300,000 and 400,000 Huguenots converted. On 15 October 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked the Edict of Nantes and ordered Protestant churches demolished. Many historians condemn it as gravely harmful to France, citing the flight of about 200,000 Huguenots; others call this an exaggeration, arguing that most leading Protestant businessmen converted and stayed. Saint-Simon criticised Louis's love of flattery, and Voltaire held that he wanted glory more than conquests themselves.
sections.last:
In 1700 Charles II of Spain died childless, leaving his empire to Louis's grandson Philip, Duke of Anjou. After weighing the partition treaties he had signed with William III, Louis accepted the will, and Anjou became Philip V. Louis then acknowledged James Stuart as king of England on the death of James II, which enraged Britain and the Dutch Republic, and in 1702 they and the Holy Roman Emperor declared war. The generals Marlborough and Eugene of Savoy checked French victories at Blenheim, Ramillies and Oudenarde. Between 1693 and 1710 over two million people died in two famines, made worse as armies foraged in the villages. By 1708 to 1709 Louis was willing to accept peace at nearly any cost, but refused the Allies' demand that he attack his own grandson. The Peace of Utrecht of 1713 and the treaties of 1714 left Philip V in Spain, gave Britain Gibraltar and Menorca and Newfoundland, Rupert's Land and Acadia, and left France in major debt.

The deaths of his son in 1711 and of two of his grandsons and a great-grandson within about a year left a five-year-old great-grandson as heir. Louis died at Versailles of gangrene on 1 September 1715, reciting a psalm. After his death the Duke of Orléans had his will, which limited the regent's power, annulled by the Parlement of Paris.
sections.legacy:
Louis's tomb at Saint-Denis was opened by revolutionaries after about 80 years, and the remains destroyed. His admirers among historians point to the expansion and more defensible frontiers of France, the reduction of aristocratic rebellion through his consolidation of royal authority, and the French culture that Europe came to emulate; they hold that his early reforms marked the birth of the modern French state. His detractors argue that his expenditure impoverished and bankrupted France, and that his failure to reform institutions led to the Revolution; his defenders reply that the state, not France, was impoverished, and that the Revolution came almost 80 years after his death.

According to Philippe de Courcillon's Journal, he told his heir on his deathbed, "I have often undertaken war too lightly and have sustained it for vanity", though some historians point out that exaggerating one's sins was a customary show of piety. Napoleon called him "the only King of France worthy of the name", Leibniz commended him, and Voltaire's The Age of Louis XIV named his reign one of the four great ages of reason and culture. The saying "I am the state" was denounced as apocryphal by the early 19th century. In 1693 he founded the Order of Saint Louis, the first decoration that could be granted to non-nobles.

summary: Louis XIV (1638–1715) became King of France at four and ruled in person from 1661, building the court at Versailles and subduing the nobility. France led Europe under him, but his wars, the persecution of Protestants and the costs of the Spanish succession war left deep debts and lasting dispute among historians.
notes: Majority: the article says Louis was declared of age on 7 September 1651, yet also speaks of his coming of age and coronation depriving the Frondeurs of their pretext, and has Mazarin in charge until 1661; both statements kept as given, no further date asserted.
Colbert: 'Controller-General of Finances in 1665' is the article's; the surplus 'by 1666' and Fouquet's fall are as in the article. Its pounds-sterling figures were left out.

Huguenot figures: 300,000 to 400,000 converted; about 200,000 emigrated (the article gives 'roughly one quarter of the Protestant population, or 1% of the French population', which are inconsistent with each other and were left out). The article states the Edict ordered churches demolished and forced baptism.
Famines: 'over two million people died in two famines' between 1693 and 1710, as in the article.
The 'hatred of Paris' is stated by the article, which elsewhere doubts the theory because Louis sponsored public works in Paris; the doubt is left out for space but the editor may want it.
Death: the article says he died four days before his 77th birthday, 'after 72 years on the throne' and gives Rohan as the priest of the last rites; the exact day of the will's annulment is not given.

Left out: Louis's mistresses and children, the Guernsey invasion, Vauban's memorandum, the dozens of fiction and film entries, the mummy and heart anecdotes, the elephant, the Edict of Versailles of 1787, Maintenon (secret marriage c. 1683-84, dated 'on or around' in the article).
The 'treaties of 1714' are Rastatt and Baden; the 'parts of Canada' are Newfoundland, Rupert's Land and Acadia as the article lists them.
References left empty for the editor.
